decks.title: Biotechnology and its Applications — Part 1: Agriculture and medicine
goals: Describe micropropagation, meristem culture and somatic hybridisation
List the advantages of GM crops and explain Bt crops, RNA interference and golden rice
Explain the production of human insulin, recombinant vaccines and the uses of stem cells

slides.heading: Biotechnology at work
slides.body_md: Part 1 — how biotechnology is used to grow better crops and make medicines.

visual.alt: Flow from tissue culture to GM crops to medicines and stem cells

slides.narration: Biotechnology helps farmers raise more food with fewer chemicals and helps doctors treat disease. We begin with plant tissue culture and genetically modified crops, then turn to medicines made by engineered microbes.

slides.heading: Plant tissue culture
slides.body_md: Any plant cell or tissue (**explant**) can regenerate a whole plant — **totipotency**. Growing explants on a sterile medium with nutrients and plant hormones allows **micropropagation**: thousands of **genetically identical** plants (**somaclones**) in a short time.

rows: Mass production of identical plants: tomato, banana, apple
Virus-free plants from apical or axillary meristems, which are free of virus: banana, sugarcane, potato
Fusion of protoplasts of two species to combine traits: pomato

visual.alt: Table of plant tissue culture techniques and uses

slides.narration: Because each plant cell carries the full set of genes, a tiny piece of tissue can give a whole new plant. Even an infected plant can yield healthy offspring, because its meristems are usually free of virus.

slides.heading: Micropropagation multiplies plants fast
slides.body_md: If each shoot gives **5** new shoots at every subculture, one explant gives **625** plantlets after **4** rounds.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: how many plantlets?
slides.body_md: A nursery starts with 3 explants of a banana variety. Each shoot gives 4 new shoots at every subculture. How many plantlets are obtained after 6 subcultures?
bullets: Plantlets $= 3 \times 4^{6}$.
All are **somaclones**, genetically identical to the parent.

visual.alt: Worked table: 12288 plantlets after 6 subcultures

slides.narration: Multiply the starting number by four for every subculture. After six rounds three explants have become more than twelve thousand plantlets, which is why tissue culture can supply whole plantations quickly.

slides.heading: Genetically modified crops
slides.body_md: Plants whose genes have been altered by manipulation are **genetically modified organisms (GMOs)**.

rows: Prevents early exhaustion of soil fertility
Golden rice rich in vitamin A

visual.alt: Table of advantages of GM crops

slides.narration: Genetic modification can make crops tolerate drought, salt or cold, resist pests without sprays, keep longer after harvest and carry more nutrients.

slides.heading: Bt crops
slides.body_md: **Bacillus thuringiensis** makes **Cry proteins** as inactive **protoxin crystals**. In the **alkaline gut** of an insect larva they dissolve and become **active toxin**, which binds the **midgut** lining and makes **pores**, so cells swell and **lyse** and the insect dies. The bacterium is not harmed because the protoxin is inactive inside it.

slides.heading: RNA interference against a nematode
slides.body_md: The nematode **Meloidogyne incognita** infects tobacco roots. Using **Agrobacterium** vectors, nematode-specific genes were introduced into tobacco so that it made both **sense and antisense RNA**. These form **double-stranded RNA**, which triggers **RNA interference (RNAi)** and **silences** a vital nematode mRNA, so the parasite cannot survive.

slides.heading: Golden rice
slides.body_md: **Golden rice** is a GM variety rich in **β-carotene** (**provitamin A**), which the body converts to **vitamin A**. It was developed to reduce **vitamin A deficiency**, which causes night blindness, in populations depending on rice.

rows: Prevent vitamin A deficiency and night blindness

visual.alt: Table about golden rice

slides.narration: Ordinary rice grains contain almost no beta-carotene. Golden rice makes it in the grain, so a staple food also supplies a vital vitamin.

slides.heading: Genetically engineered insulin
slides.body_md: Insulin has **two chains, A and B**, linked by **disulphide bridges**. In the body it is made as **proinsulin** with an extra **C peptide**, which is removed. In **1983 Eli Lilly** prepared two DNA sequences for chains **A and B**, put them into **E. coli plasmids**, produced the chains **separately**, and joined them by **disulphide bonds**.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: the insulin molecule
slides.body_md: Chain A of insulin has 21 amino acids and chain B has 30. How many amino acids does mature insulin have, and why was the C peptide not made in the genetically engineered method?

Bone-marrow transplant for leukaemia; repairing damaged tissue
Replacing damaged tissues, research on spinal-cord injury and diabetes

decks.title: Biotechnology and its Applications — Part 2: Gene therapy, diagnosis, transgenic animals and ethics
goals: Describe gene therapy for ADA deficiency (SCID)
Explain molecular diagnosis by PCR, ELISA and DNA or RNA probes
Give the uses of transgenic animals, and explain the role of GEAC, biopiracy and biopatents

slides.heading: Healing, testing and the questions it raises
slides.body_md: Part 2 — correcting faulty genes, detecting disease early, using transgenic animals, and the ethics of it all.

visual.alt: Flow from gene therapy to diagnosis to transgenic animals to ethics

slides.narration: Biotechnology can now correct some genetic defects, find infections before symptoms appear, and use animals to make medicines. These powers also raise questions of safety, fairness and ownership.

slides.heading: Gene therapy for ADA deficiency
slides.body_md: **Gene therapy** corrects a gene defect by delivering a **normal gene** into a person. The first clinical gene therapy (**1990**) treated a four-year-old girl with **adenosine deaminase (ADA) deficiency**, which causes **severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID)**.

nodes.label: Collect lymphocytes from the patient’s blood
Introduce functional ADA cDNA with a retroviral vector
Return the lymphocytes to the patient

visual.alt: Flow of gene therapy for ADA deficiency

slides.narration: Lymphocytes do not live for ever, so the treatment must be repeated periodically. If the normal ADA gene is put into bone-marrow cells at an early embryonic stage, it could give a permanent cure.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: how many cells were corrected?
slides.body_md: In a gene-therapy trial, 200 million lymphocytes were treated with the retroviral vector and 30 million took up the functional ADA gene. What percentage was corrected, and why must the treatment be repeated?
bullets: Corrected $= \dfrac{30}{200} \times 100 = 15$ percent.
Mature lymphocytes are **not immortal**, so the corrected cells die out and fresh infusions are needed.

visual.alt: Worked table: 15 percent of lymphocytes corrected

slides.narration: Only a fraction of cells take up the gene, but even these can restore some immune function. Because they eventually die, the patient needs repeated treatment unless stem cells are corrected.

slides.heading: Molecular diagnosis
slides.body_md: Early diagnosis is not possible by conventional methods such as serum and urine analysis. Molecular methods detect pathogens or mutations **when they are still few**.

rows: Amplifies very small amounts of DNA or RNA
HIV in suspected AIDS patients; mutations in suspected cancer
Detects the pathogen’s antigens or antibodies against it
Labelled single-stranded nucleic acid hybridises with its complement
Detects a mutated gene: no signal on autoradiography where the probe cannot pair

visual.alt: Table of methods of molecular diagnosis

slides.narration: PCR can find a pathogen before symptoms appear. A radioactive probe binds only to a complementary sequence; if a gene is mutated, the probe cannot pair, and the band is missing from the photographic film.

slides.heading: Quick check: ADA
slides.body_md: Deficiency of which enzyme was treated by the first clinical gene therapy?
slides.narration: Quick check. Its lack causes severe combined immunodeficiency.

slides.heading: Transgenic animals
slides.body_md: **Transgenic animals** have had their DNA manipulated to carry and express an **extra (foreign) gene**. Over 95 percent of existing transgenic animals are **mice**; others include rats, rabbits, pigs, sheep, cows and fish.

rows: Models for cancer, cystic fibrosis, rheumatoid arthritis, Alzheimer’s disease
α-1-antitrypsin to treat emphysema; human α-lactalbumin in milk
Polio vaccine tested on transgenic mice
Toxicity testing with animals sensitive to toxic substances

visual.alt: Table of uses of transgenic animals

slides.narration: Transgenic animals let scientists see how a gene works inside a living body, and test new treatments. Some make valuable human proteins in their milk, which can be collected without harming the animal.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: Rosie the cow
slides.body_md: In **1997** the first transgenic cow, **Rosie**, produced milk with human **α-lactalbumin** at about **2.4 g per litre** — nutritionally more balanced for human babies. How much of the protein was in 15 litres of her milk?
bullets: Protein $= 2.4 \times 15 = 36$ g.
The milk could be used to feed **human babies** better than ordinary cow milk.

visual.alt: Worked table: 36 grams in 15 litres

slides.narration: Multiply the concentration by the volume. Animals such as Rosie act as living factories for human proteins, which is sometimes called pharming.

slides.heading: Biosafety, GEAC and biopatents
slides.body_md: Genetic modification raises **ethical** and **safety** questions. In India, the **Genetic Engineering Appraisal Committee (GEAC)** decides on the **validity of GM research** and the **safety of introducing GM organisms** for public services.

rows: Unpredictable effects of GM organisms on the ecosystem and health
A patent granted for biological entities, products or processes
Use of bio-resources by companies without proper authorisation or compensation to the countries and people concerned

slides.narration: Patents encourage research, but they can also let companies claim ownership of plants and knowledge that communities developed over centuries. Laws are needed so that the people who preserved these resources share the benefits.

notes.title: Biotechnology and its Applications — Notes

sections.heading: 1. Tissue culture, somatic hybridisation and GM crops
sections.body_md:
**Plant tissue culture:** whole plants can be regenerated from **explants** (any part of a plant) grown in **sterile** conditions on special nutrient media — the capacity called **totipotency**. The medium provides a carbon source (sucrose), inorganic salts, vitamins, amino acids and **growth regulators** such as auxins and cytokinins.
- **Micropropagation** produces thousands of plants in a short time; each plant is genetically identical to the original — a **somaclone** (here, 5 shoots per subculture give 625 plantlets after 4 rounds). Used for tomato, banana, apple and others.
- **Meristem culture:** although a plant is infected with a virus, its **apical and axillary meristems are free of virus**; culturing them gives **virus-free plants** (banana, sugarcane, potato).
- **Somatic hybridisation:** single cells are isolated, their walls digested by **cellulase and pectinase** to give naked **protoplasts**, and protoplasts of two varieties or species are **fused** to give **hybrid protoplasts**, which are grown into **somatic hybrids** — for example the **pomato** (tomato + potato), though it did not combine all the desired traits.

**Genetically modified (GM) crops** — plants, bacteria, fungi and animals whose genes have been altered by manipulation are GMOs. GM plants: (i) are more **tolerant to abiotic stresses** (cold, drought, salt, heat); (ii) **reduce reliance on chemical pesticides** (pest-resistant crops); (iii) **reduce post-harvest losses**; (iv) **increase efficiency of mineral use** (preventing early exhaustion of soil fertility); (v) have **enhanced nutritional value** (golden rice); (vi) can provide **alternative resources** — starches, fuels and pharmaceuticals.

sections.heading: 2. Pest-resistant and nutritionally enhanced crops
sections.body_md:
**Bt crops:** some strains of ***Bacillus thuringiensis*** produce proteins that kill certain insects such as **lepidopterans** (tobacco budworm, armyworm), **coleopterans** (beetles) and **dipterans** (flies, mosquitoes). The bacterium forms protein crystals containing a toxic **insecticidal protein** that exists as an **inactive protoxin**. When an insect ingests it, the **alkaline pH of the gut** solubilises the crystals and converts the protoxin to the **active toxin**, which binds to the **surface of midgut epithelial cells** and creates **pores**, causing **swelling and lysis** and death of the insect. The toxin is coded by **cry** genes: **cryIAc** and **cryIIAb** control **cotton bollworms**; **cryIAb** controls the **corn borer**. Bt cotton, Bt corn, rice, tomato, potato and soybean have been developed.

**RNA interference against nematodes:** the nematode ***Meloidogyne incognita*** infects the roots of **tobacco** and reduces yield. Using ***Agrobacterium*** vectors, nematode-specific genes were introduced into the host plant so that it produced **both sense and complementary antisense RNA**. These form **double-stranded RNA (dsRNA)**, which starts **RNAi** and **silences** the specific mRNA of the nematode; the parasite cannot survive in the transgenic host. RNAi is a method of **cellular defence** in all eukaryotes.

**Golden rice:** a GM variety containing **β-carotene (provitamin A)**, giving grains a golden colour, to combat **vitamin A deficiency** and night blindness.

GM rice rich in β-carotene (provitamin A).

sections.heading: 3. Insulin, vaccines and stem cells
sections.body_md:
**Genetically engineered insulin:** insulin used for diabetes was earlier extracted from the **pancreas of slaughtered cattle and pigs**, and some patients developed **allergies** to the foreign protein. Insulin consists of **two short polypeptide chains, A and B**, linked by **disulphide bridges**. In mammals it is synthesised as a **pro-hormone (proinsulin)** with an extra stretch, the **C peptide**, which is removed during maturation. In **1983**, the American company **Eli Lilly** prepared **two DNA sequences** corresponding to chains **A and B** of human insulin and introduced them into **plasmids of *E. coli***; the chains were produced **separately**, extracted and **combined by creating disulphide bonds** to form human insulin.

**Vaccines:** recombinant DNA technology allows production of antigenic polypeptides in bacteria or yeast; for example the **hepatitis B vaccine** produced in **yeast**. Such vaccines are safer because they contain no live pathogen.

**Stem cells** are **undifferentiated** cells that can **renew themselves** by division and **differentiate** into specialised cells. **Embryonic stem cells** (from the inner cell mass of an early embryo) are **pluripotent** and can form almost any cell type. **Adult stem cells** (bone marrow, umbilical cord blood) are **multipotent**. Applications: **bone-marrow transplants** for leukaemia and other blood disorders, replacing **damaged tissues**, and research into **spinal-cord injuries, diabetes** and other diseases; **cord-blood banking** stores stem cells for future use.

Able to form almost any cell type.

sections.heading: 4. Gene therapy and molecular diagnosis
sections.body_md:
**Gene therapy** is a collection of methods that allows correction of a gene defect diagnosed in a child or embryo: genes are inserted into a person’s cells and tissues to treat a disease, a normal gene compensating for the non-functional one. The **first clinical gene therapy** was given in **1990** to a four-year-old girl with **adenosine deaminase (ADA) deficiency**. ADA is crucial for the immune system; its deletion causes **severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID)**. Treatment can be by bone-marrow transplantation or enzyme-replacement therapy (injection of functional ADA), but these are not completely curative. In gene therapy, **lymphocytes** from the patient’s blood are grown in culture, a functional **ADA cDNA** is introduced using a **retroviral vector**, and the cells are **returned** to the patient. As these cells are **not immortal**, periodic infusion is needed. If the gene isolated from **marrow cells** producing ADA is introduced into cells at **early embryonic stages**, it could be a **permanent cure**.

**Molecular diagnosis:** conventional methods (serum and urine analysis) cannot detect a pathogen early. Recombinant DNA technology, **PCR** and **ELISA** allow **early diagnosis**:
- **PCR** detects very **low concentrations** of a pathogen by amplifying its nucleic acid — used to detect **HIV** in suspected AIDS patients and **mutations** in genes of suspected cancer patients.
- A **single-stranded DNA or RNA probe**, tagged with a **radioactive** molecule, is allowed to **hybridise** to its complementary DNA in a clone of cells, followed by **autoradiography**; a clone with a **mutated** gene does **not** appear on the film, because the probe is not complementary to it.
- **ELISA** is based on **antigen–antibody interaction**; infection can be detected by the presence of **antigens** (proteins, glycoproteins) or of **antibodies** synthesised against the pathogen.

sections.heading: 5. Transgenic animals
sections.body_md:
Animals that have had their DNA manipulated to possess and express an **extra (foreign) gene** are **transgenic animals**. Transgenic rats, rabbits, pigs, sheep, cows and fish have been produced, though **over 95 percent** of all existing transgenic animals are **mice**.

**Uses:**
- **Normal physiology and development:** studying how genes are regulated and how they affect body functions (for example, insulin-like growth factor).
- **Study of disease:** models for human diseases such as **cancer, cystic fibrosis, rheumatoid arthritis and Alzheimer’s disease**, so that new treatments can be investigated.
- **Biological products:** medicines can be expensive to make; transgenic animals that produce useful products are introduced with the gene coding for the product — for example human protein **α-1-antitrypsin**, used to treat **emphysema**; products for **phenylketonuria (PKU)** and **cystic fibrosis** are being tried. In **1997** the first transgenic cow, **Rosie**, produced **human protein-enriched milk (2.4 g per litre)** containing **human α-lactalbumin**, nutritionally more balanced for human babies than natural cow milk.
- **Vaccine safety:** transgenic mice are used to test the safety of vaccines (for example **polio vaccine**) before use on humans.
- **Chemical safety testing (toxicity testing):** transgenic animals carrying genes that make them **more sensitive** to toxic substances give results in less time.

sections.heading: 6. Biosafety, ethics, biopiracy and biopatents
sections.body_md:
Manipulation of living organisms raises **ethical** and **biosafety** concerns: GM organisms may have **unpredictable effects** when introduced into an ecosystem. The Indian Government has set up organisations such as **GEAC (Genetic Engineering Appraisal Committee)**, which makes decisions regarding the **validity of GM research** and the **safety of introducing GM organisms** for public services.

**Biopatents** are patents granted for biological entities and for products derived from them. Some companies have been granted patents on products and technologies that use genetic materials, plants and other biological resources **long identified, developed and used** by farmers and indigenous people of a country.

**Biopiracy** is the term used to refer to the **use of bio-resources by multinational companies** and other organisations **without proper authorisation** from the countries and people concerned and **without compensatory payment**.
- **Basmati rice:** India has about **27 documented varieties** of basmati, distinct for unique aroma and flavour. In **1997** an American company obtained patent rights on basmati rice through the **US Patent and Trademark Office**, for a “new” variety derived from Indian farmers’ varieties crossed with semi-dwarf varieties.
- Attempts have also been made to patent uses, products and processes based on Indian traditional herbal medicines such as **turmeric** and **neem**.
Most industrialised nations are rich financially but poor in biodiversity and traditional knowledge, while developing nations are rich in both. The Indian Parliament has cleared the second amendment of the **Indian Patents Bill** to take such issues into consideration, including emergency provisions and research and development initiatives.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Saying Bt toxin is active inside the bacterium (it is an inactive protoxin until the alkaline insect gut).
- Mixing up the cry genes: cryIAc and cryIIAb (cotton bollworms), cryIAb (corn borer).
- Saying RNAi adds a protein to kill the nematode (it silences a nematode mRNA).
- Writing that genetically engineered insulin was made as proinsulin (chains A and B were made separately).
- Calling gene therapy for ADA permanent (lymphocytes die; repeated infusions are needed).
- Confusing biopatent with biopiracy.

- 1-mark subparts: a cry gene, a vector, an enzyme for protoplasts, GEAC in full, a transgenic product.
- 2–3-mark questions: micropropagation and meristem culture; Bt toxin action; RNAi; insulin production; gene therapy; probes.
- 5-mark questions in parts: GM crops with Bt and RNAi; medical applications; transgenic animals with ethics and biopiracy.

questions.stem_md: What is micropropagation? Give two of its advantages.

answer.model_answer_md: **Micropropagation** is the production of a **large number of plants** in a short time by **tissue culture** of explants on a sterile nutrient medium with growth regulators. Advantages: the plants are **genetically identical (somaclones)** to a good parent; **many plants** are obtained **quickly**, at any season, and from little material.

questions.stem_md: Describe the steps of somatic hybridisation and name one somatic hybrid.

answer.model_answer_md: Single cells of two plants are isolated, and their walls are digested with **cellulase and pectinase** to give naked **protoplasts**. Protoplasts of the **two varieties or species** are **fused** (for example with polyethylene glycol) to form **hybrid protoplasts**. These are cultured on a nutrient medium to regenerate a **somatic hybrid** plant. Example: the **pomato**, from **tomato and potato**.

questions.stem_md: A state agriculture department is deciding whether to promote GM crops. Give three benefits of GM crops it should consider, with an example of each.

answer.model_answer_md: (i) **Tolerance to abiotic stresses** — varieties tolerant to **drought, salt, cold or heat**. (ii) **Less use of chemical pesticides** — **Bt cotton** resists bollworms. (iii) **Higher nutritional value** — **golden rice** rich in vitamin A. (Also: fewer **post-harvest losses**, more efficient **mineral use**, **alternative resources** such as starch and fuels.)

questions.solution_md: Three benefits.

questions.stem_md:
(a) What is meant by totipotency? [1]
(b) Describe micropropagation and explain how meristem culture gives virus-free plants. [2]
(c) A nursery needs 1000 identical plantlets of a rare tree from one explant; each shoot gives 4 new shoots per subculture. How many subcultures are needed at least? [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Totipotency** is the capacity of a plant cell or explant to **regenerate a whole plant**.

(b) Explants are grown on a **sterile nutrient medium** with **growth regulators**; shoots form and are **subcultured** repeatedly, then **rooted** and **hardened** to give many **somaclones**. Although an infected plant carries virus, its **apical and axillary meristems are free of virus**, so plants raised from them are **virus-free**.

(c) After k subcultures there are $4^{k}$ plantlets: $4^{4} = 256 < 1000$ and $4^{5} = 1024 \ge 1000$, so **5 subcultures** are needed.

**Reason (R):** The protein exists in the bacterium as an inactive protoxin, which becomes active only in the alkaline gut of an insect.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, and the inactive protoxin explains why the bacterium is unharmed — option (a).

cryIAb only
ADA and lacZ
ampᴿ and tetᴿ

The insect lacks a midgut altogether.
Bt cotton makes the toxin only in roots.
The acid converts the toxin into a vitamin.

questions.solution_md: Activation of the crystal protoxin needs the alkaline pH of the insect gut — option (a).

cotton

questions.stem_md: Many children in a rice-eating community suffer from night blindness. Which GM crop was developed to address this problem?

options.text_md: Bt cotton
RNAi tobacco
Flavr Savr tomato
Golden rice, rich in β-carotene

questions.solution_md: β-carotene is converted to vitamin A, preventing night blindness — option (d).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Transgenic tobacco designed against Meloidogyne produces both sense and antisense RNA of a nematode gene.

**Reason (R):** Agrobacterium is a pathogen of dicot plants.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, but Agrobacterium being a pathogen does not explain why sense and antisense RNA are made (they form dsRNA for RNAi) — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Explain how the Bt toxin kills a bollworm larva that feeds on Bt cotton.

answer.model_answer_md: The larva swallows **Cry protein crystals** in the form of an **inactive protoxin**. The **alkaline pH** of its gut **solubilises** the crystals and converts them to the **active toxin**, which binds the **midgut epithelial cells** and creates **pores**, causing the cells to **swell and lyse**; the larva dies.

questions.solution_md: Activation and pore formation.

questions.stem_md: Why would golden rice be especially useful in poor communities that depend on rice, and what nutrient does it supply?

answer.model_answer_md: Ordinary rice grains contain almost **no β-carotene**, so people who eat mainly rice and little vegetables suffer **vitamin A deficiency** and **night blindness**. Golden rice makes **β-carotene (provitamin A)** in its grains, which the body converts to **vitamin A**, through a food they already eat.

questions.solution_md: β-carotene; vitamin A.

marking_scheme.step: Vitamin A deficiency in rice diets

questions.stem_md: A tobacco farmer’s crop is stunted by root-knot nematodes (Meloidogyne incognita). Scientists offer her a transgenic tobacco variety whose roots the nematode cannot survive in. Explain the RNA-interference strategy behind this variety.

answer.model_answer_md: Using ***Agrobacterium*** vectors, **nematode-specific genes** were introduced into tobacco. The transgenic plant produced **both sense and antisense RNA** of these genes. The two complementary RNAs formed **double-stranded RNA (dsRNA)**, which started **RNA interference** and **silenced** the specific **mRNA of the nematode**. The nematode could not make a vital protein and **could not survive** in the transgenic host.

questions.solution_md: Vector, dsRNA, silencing.

marking_scheme.step: Sense and antisense RNA form dsRNA

questions.stem_md:
(a) Describe the mode of action of the Bt toxin, naming the cry genes used for cotton and maize. [3]
(b) Explain how RNA interference protects tobacco from a nematode. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) ***Bacillus thuringiensis*** forms **crystals** of an **inactive protoxin**. In the **alkaline gut** of an insect larva the crystals **dissolve** and the protoxin becomes the **active toxin**, which binds the **midgut epithelium** and makes **pores**; the cells **swell and lyse** and the larva dies. **cryIAc** and **cryIIAb** protect **cotton** against **bollworms**; **cryIAb** protects **maize** against the **corn borer**.

(b) Nematode-specific genes are introduced by ***Agrobacterium*** so that the plant makes **sense and antisense RNA**; these form **dsRNA**, which triggers **RNAi** and **silences** a vital **nematode mRNA**, so ***Meloidogyne incognita*** cannot survive.

questions.solution_md: Bt; RNAi.

questions.stem_md: Insulin is first made in the pancreas as proinsulin. Which part is removed to give mature insulin?

options.text_md: Chain A
Chain B
The disulphide bridges
The C peptide

questions.solution_md: The C peptide is removed during maturation — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Why did Eli Lilly make the A and B chains of human insulin separately in E. coli instead of making proinsulin?

options.text_md: E. coli cannot make any protein longer than 30 amino acids.
Producing the two chains separately and joining them avoided the need to remove the C peptide.
Chain A is toxic to bacteria.
Disulphide bridges form only inside bacteria.

questions.solution_md: The chains were joined chemically by disulphide bonds, skipping C-peptide removal — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Before 1983, some diabetic patients reacted badly to their insulin injections. What was the main reason?

options.text_md: The insulin contained Bt toxin.
The insulin was made by E. coli and contained bacteria.
The insulin came from cattle and pigs and was a foreign protein that could trigger allergies.
The insulin lacked chain A.

questions.solution_md: Animal insulin can provoke allergic or immune reactions — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A child is given a hepatitis B vaccine made by yeast cells carrying a viral gene. Why is this vaccine considered safe?

options.text_md: The yeast kills the virus inside the child.
It contains antibodies from another person.
It contains only a viral surface protein, not the infectious virus.
It is made from dead hepatitis patients’ blood.

questions.solution_md: A recombinant antigenic protein cannot cause infection — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Which property makes embryonic stem cells more versatile than adult stem cells?

options.text_md: They are pluripotent and can form almost any cell type.
They cannot divide.
They have already become nerve cells.
They contain no DNA.

questions.solution_md: Embryonic stem cells are pluripotent; adult stem cells are multipotent — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Parents store their newborn’s umbilical cord blood in a bank. What is the main purpose?

options.text_md: It supplies insulin for diabetes.
It is a rich source of stem cells that may later be used to treat blood disorders.
It provides Bt toxin for vaccines.
It is used to make golden rice.

questions.solution_md: Cord blood contains stem cells for future therapy — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Chain A of insulin has 21 amino acids and chain B has 30. How many peptide bonds are there in the two chains together?
questions.solution_md: A chain of $n$ amino acids has $n - 1$ peptide bonds: $(21 - 1) + (30 - 1) = 49$.

questions.stem_md: What are stem cells? Distinguish embryonic from adult stem cells.

answer.model_answer_md: **Stem cells** are **undifferentiated** cells that can **renew themselves** and **differentiate** into specialised cells. **Embryonic** stem cells, from the early embryo, are **pluripotent** and can form almost any cell type. **Adult** stem cells, as in **bone marrow** or cord blood, are **multipotent** and form a limited range of cells.

questions.solution_md: Definition; two types.

questions.stem_md: Describe how human insulin was produced by recombinant DNA technology, and give one advantage over insulin from animals.

answer.model_answer_md: In **1983 Eli Lilly** prepared **two DNA sequences** coding for **chains A and B** of human insulin. These were introduced into **plasmids** of ***E. coli***, which produced the **two chains separately**. The chains were **extracted** and **combined by creating disulphide bonds**, giving human insulin. Advantage: it is **identical to human insulin**, so it does not cause the **allergic reactions** that some patients had to **cattle or pig insulin**, and it can be made in **large amounts**.

questions.solution_md: Steps; advantage.

marking_scheme.step: Two DNA sequences for A and B
Made in E. coli; joined by disulphide bonds

questions.stem_md: The first clinical gene therapy, in 1990, treated a girl who lacked which enzyme?

options.text_md: β-galactosidase
Adenosine deaminase (ADA)
Reverse transcriptase
Taq polymerase

questions.solution_md: ADA deficiency causes SCID — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Why does a deficiency of adenosine deaminase lead to severe combined immunodeficiency?

options.text_md: ADA digests all bacteria in the blood.
ADA is crucial for the immune system; without it lymphocytes do not function properly.
ADA is a hormone that controls blood sugar.
ADA makes red blood cells carry oxygen.

questions.solution_md: Lack of ADA damages immune cells, causing SCID — option (b).

questions.stem_md: In gene therapy for ADA deficiency, which vector was used to introduce the functional ADA cDNA into the patient’s lymphocytes?

options.text_md: A retroviral vector
The Ti plasmid of Agrobacterium
A yeast artificial chromosome
A Bt crystal

questions.solution_md: A disarmed retrovirus delivered the gene — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Doctors want a permanent cure for ADA deficiency instead of repeated infusions of corrected lymphocytes. Which approach would achieve this?

options.text_md: Giving more antibiotics
Infusing corrected red blood cells
Introducing the ADA gene into bone-marrow stem cells at an early stage
Vaccinating the child against SCID

questions.solution_md: Corrected stem cells keep producing functional lymphocytes — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A radioactive probe complementary to a normal gene is hybridised with DNA from several clones. On the autoradiograph, one clone shows no band. What does this suggest?

options.text_md: That clone has the most copies of the normal gene.
The probe was destroyed by that clone.
That clone carries a mutated gene to which the probe cannot pair.
That clone is the positive control.

questions.solution_md: A probe binds only complementary sequences; a mutated gene gives no signal — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A person exposed to HIV a few weeks ago has no symptoms and a negative antibody test. Which technique could detect the virus at this early stage?

options.text_md: Urine analysis
PCR, which amplifies very small amounts of viral nucleic acid
Gel electrophoresis without amplification
Micropropagation

questions.solution_md: PCR detects pathogens at very low concentrations — option (b).

questions.stem_md: ELISA detects infection through the interaction between an antigen and an ______.
questions.solution_md: Antibody.

questions.stem_md: In a gene-therapy trial, 300 million of a patient’s lymphocytes were treated with the vector and 45 million expressed the ADA gene. What percentage of the treated cells were corrected?
questions.solution_md: $\dfrac{45}{300} \times 100 = 15$ percent.

questions.stem_md: Why are molecular methods better than conventional methods for early diagnosis of infection? Name two such methods.

answer.model_answer_md: Conventional methods such as **serum and urine analysis** detect a pathogen only after it has **multiplied** and caused **symptoms**. Molecular methods detect it at **very low concentrations**, **before symptoms appear**, so treatment can start early. Examples: **PCR** and **ELISA** (also DNA or RNA **probes**).

questions.solution_md: Early detection; examples.

questions.stem_md: Describe the gene therapy given to a child with ADA deficiency, and explain why it is not a permanent cure.

answer.model_answer_md: **Lymphocytes** are taken from the patient’s **blood** and grown in **culture**. A functional **ADA cDNA** is introduced into them using a **retroviral vector**, and the corrected lymphocytes are **returned** to the patient, where they make ADA and restore immunity. It is **not permanent** because these lymphocytes are **not immortal**; they die and **periodic infusions** are needed. A permanent cure would need the gene introduced into **bone-marrow stem cells** at an early stage.

questions.solution_md: Steps; not permanent.

marking_scheme.step: ADA cDNA by retroviral vector; returned

questions.stem_md: A family has a history of a single-gene disorder. Explain how a labelled DNA probe and autoradiography could show which relatives carry the mutated gene.

answer.model_answer_md: A **single-stranded DNA probe** complementary to the **normal gene** is labelled with a **radioactive** molecule. DNA from each relative is allowed to **hybridise** with the probe and the result is exposed to film (**autoradiography**). Where the gene is **normal**, the probe **pairs** and a **band** appears; where both copies are **mutated**, the probe **cannot pair**, so **no band** appears (a reduced signal in a carrier). Relatives can thus be identified **before** symptoms appear.

questions.solution_md: Probe hybridisation; missing band.

questions.stem_md:
(a) What is gene therapy? [1]
(b) Describe the first clinical gene therapy, naming the disorder and the vector used. [2]
(c) Explain how PCR and a labelled probe help in early molecular diagnosis. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Gene therapy** is the correction of a gene defect by **delivering a normal gene** into a person’s cells to compensate for a non-functional one.

(b) In **1990** a four-year-old girl with **ADA deficiency** (causing **SCID**) was treated: her **lymphocytes** were grown in culture, a functional **ADA cDNA** was introduced with a **retroviral vector**, and the cells were **returned** to her; infusions were **repeated** because lymphocytes are not immortal.

(c) **PCR** amplifies **very small amounts** of a pathogen’s nucleic acid, detecting infection (such as **HIV**) or **mutations** before symptoms. A **radioactive single-stranded probe** hybridises with complementary DNA; after **autoradiography**, a **mutated** gene gives **no signal** because the probe cannot pair.

questions.solution_md: Definition; ADA therapy; diagnosis.

To cure polio in mice

questions.stem_md: Milk from a transgenic cow contains 2.4 g of a human protein per litre. How many grams of the protein are in 12 litres of milk?
What are transgenic animals? State two ways in which they help in studying human diseases or making medicines.

answer.model_answer_md: **Transgenic animals** carry and express an **extra (foreign) gene** introduced by manipulating their DNA. They serve as **models** of human diseases such as **cancer, cystic fibrosis and Alzheimer’s disease**, so treatments can be studied; and they **produce human proteins** such as **α-1-antitrypsin** (for emphysema) in their milk.

questions.solution_md: Definition; two uses.

questions.stem_md: A pharmaceutical company plans to produce a scarce human enzyme in the milk of transgenic goats. Explain why this is attractive, and name two other uses of transgenic animals.

answer.model_answer_md: Making complex human proteins chemically or in cell cultures is **expensive**; a transgenic goat carrying the **human gene** secretes the protein into its **milk**, which can be collected **continuously without harming** the animal (as Rosie’s milk carried **α-lactalbumin**). Other uses: testing **vaccine safety** (for example polio vaccine in transgenic mice) and **toxicity testing** of chemicals; also **disease models** and study of **normal physiology**.

questions.solution_md: Pharming; other uses.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Define transgenic animals and name the animal most commonly used. [1]
(b) Describe four uses of transgenic animals with examples. [3]
(c) What was special about the milk of Rosie? [1]
